characters: Awuku: a cheerful nine-year-old Ghanaian boy with short neat hair, wearing a green-and-khaki school uniform.
Jamila: his practical nine-year-old female classmate wearing a matching green-and-khaki school dress and a tidy white headscarf.
Their teacher: a supportive Ghanaian male teacher in a neat short-sleeved cream shirt and khaki trousers.

narrationPlan.voice: A cheerful voice for Awuku; a practical, bright voice for Jamila
narrationPlan.pace: Steady, with a bit of humour about the smell (about 90 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with a different voice for each character.
Pause for two seconds at each question activity.
Never rush the last page: let the ending land.

music: A light, bouncing tune with a shovel beat (placeholder)
culturalNotes: Many Ghanaian farms and school gardens enrich soil with plant trimmings and peelings; separating plastic sachets and wrappers keeps soil healthy and drains clear.
Hygiene and safety rules: keep meat, bones, glass, and plastic out of school compost, site heaps away from water points, and wash hands with soap after gardening.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?

teacherGuide.overview: A practical school-garden story demonstrating how biodegradable plant waste decomposes into nutrient-rich compost while plastic persists, motivating waste sorting and handwashing.
learningGoals: Explain simply what compost is and how soil organisms make it.
Sort common school waste into compostable plant matter vs. non-compostable waste.
Follow hygiene rules including covering the heap and washing hands with soap.

beforeReading: Ask: after break time, what happens to banana peels compared with plastic wrappers?
whileReading: Pause on page 4 and ask learners to name the soil helpers that break peels down.
afterReading: Sort ten safe classroom items (or picture cards) into “Compost Heap” and “Waste Bin”.
Observe a small covered compost bucket of leaves and fruit peels over four weeks.
discussion: Why did the peels turn into dark soil food while plastic wrappers stayed unchanged?
Why did Awuku and Jamila cover the heap with dry leaves and wash their hands afterwards?
reflection: What is one simple way you can help keep your school compound or home yard cleaner this week?

support: Sort picture cards of banana peels, dry leaves, plastic bottles, and sweet wrappers onto two coloured mats.
stretch: Measure the height of a leaf-and-peel jar each Friday for four weeks and record how it settles as it rots.

culturalNotes: Many Ghanaian farms and school gardens enrich soil with plant trimmings and peelings; separating plastic sachets and wrappers keeps soil healthy and drains clear.
Hygiene and safety rules: keep meat, bones, glass, and plastic out of school compost, site heaps away from water points, and wash hands with soap after gardening.
localiseThis: Use familiar local peelings such as plantain, banana, orange, mango, and cassava/yam skins (well covered).
Keep compost pits well away from boreholes or wells, and wash hands with soap and running water every time.

factCheck.claim: Earthworms and soil microorganisms decompose plant peels and dry leaves into nutrient-rich compost, whereas conventional plastics do not rot into soil.
factCheck.explanation: Decomposers break down organic plant tissues into humus and mineral nutrients for plants, while synthetic plastic polymers resist natural biological breakdown.
